page.text:
The `Documented:` section is used to document information about the
concept being defined. Either a `called:` or a `written:` item needs to
be specified.

The `called:` section's text is interpreted as non-math mode LaTeX and
allows you to specify what the construct is called when spoken aloud.
More than one item can be specified if there is more than one way to
describe the item.

The `written:` section's text is interpreted as math mode LaTeX and
allows you to specify what the construct looks like when written on
paper.

If only one of `written:` or `called:` is provided, the other item is
automatically generated as the same value. So in the example above
`called:` specifies that one says "set" when specifying the construct
and because `written:` is omitted, one would also write "set".

To make this more clear, consider the following example:

```mlg-fragment
[\function:on{A}:to{B}]
Describes: f(x__) ::= y_
...
Documented:
. called: "function on $A?$ to $B?$"
. written: "f? \: : \: A? \rightarrow B?"
...
```

We'll gloss over some details here, but at a high level, a type name can
have inputs, here `A` and `B`, and a `?` is used to refer to them in the
`Documented:` section.

Here the `called:` and `written:` sections communicate that if one had `g
is \function:on{X}:to{Y}`, then to describe that out loud one would say
"g is a function on $X$ to $Y$". To express the same thing written
down, one would write $g \: : \: X \rightarrow Y$. Further uses of
`Documented:` will be covered in more detail later.
